title: The good shepherd (John 10:11–18)
hook: he knows his sheep and lays down his life

segments.voice: Yesterday, a sheepfold with a gap in the wall, and Jesus saying: I am the door. Your line was life to the full. What abundant thing did you choose? Day six hundred twenty.

Go down into the catacombs under Rome, the underground burial passages of the early Christians, and look at the painted walls. Long before the cross became the most common Christian image, one picture shows up again and again: a young man with a sheep across his shoulders, holding its legs in front of his chest. Some of these paintings go back to the two hundreds, the third century. When the first Christians wanted to picture Jesus near the graves of the people they loved, this is the picture many of them chose. It comes from today's words.

"I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep." This is the fourth I am saying in John, right on the heels of the door. The word for good is kalos, which means good and also beautiful, noble, the real thing. Not just a shepherd who does the job. The shepherd as he ought to be. Jesus sets him beside someone else: the hired hand. The hireling, as the King James calls him, sees a wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and runs. Not because he's evil. Because they're not his sheep. He's paid by the day. The good shepherd stays, because they're his own. And then a line of real tenderness: "I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine." Knowing goes both ways. He knows them, and they know him. Shepherding pictures run deep in the scriptures Jesus grew up with. King David was a shepherd. Psalm twenty-three begins, the Lord is my shepherd. In Ezekiel, God condemns shepherds who feed themselves instead of the flock, and promises to search for the lost sheep himself. Jesus steps into that old picture. He adds: "And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold." Christians have long read that as a sign the flock would grow wider than anyone listening expected. And the most striking part: he says no one takes his life from him. "I lay it down of myself." The good shepherd isn't caught off guard. He chooses to give his life for the sheep, freely.
screen: then, large: `I LAY IT DOWN OF MYSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: know someone's name and use it. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people you see often but don't really know. The person at the coffee shop. A neighbor. The security guard. Someone at work you nod to. Do you know their names? Pick one person whose name you know, or would like to learn. Picture saying it to them, warmly, today. Then remember a time someone used your name when you didn't expect them to know it, and how that felt. If you pray, you can give thanks that you're known by name. If you don't, just hold the feeling of being known. The bell holds the time.
Hireling. The hired hand who runs when the wolf comes, because the sheep aren't his own, unlike the good shepherd who stays and lays down his life.
Your line: I know my own. Today, learn one name you didn't know, or use one you did, and look the person in the eye when you say it. Day six hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Many churches keep a Good Shepherd Sunday in the Easter season, and the image of Christ carrying a sheep remains common in stained glass, children's Bibles and church art.

fork.setup: you're watching the flock for pay. a wolf comes over the hill. what does the hireling in the story do?
fork.reveal: the hireling flees, because the sheep aren't his. the good shepherd stays and gives his life for them.

original.note: Greek: good, beautiful, noble. The shepherd as a shepherd ought to be.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle picture of Jesus with a lamb.
what it means: the shepherd who knows each sheep, stays when the wolf comes, and chooses to lay down his life.
what a scholar hears: kalos means both good and beautiful, and the image draws on Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34, where God promises to shepherd the flock himself.

notes: Good Shepherd images in the Roman catacombs (e.g., Catacomb of Callixtus, Priscilla) dated to the 3rd century; the cross became common in Christian art later (4th–5th centuries). Confirm phrasing.
'Psalm twenty-three begins, the Lord is my shepherd' is unmarked KJV wording; could be added to sources as a quotation. Confirm.
'Other sheep' (10:16) is read by many as Gentiles; the script says 'the flock would grow wider than anyone listening expected'. Confirm.
Good Shepherd Sunday: fourth Sunday of Easter (Catholic, many Anglican/Lutheran); confirm.
